analytic.title: Towards an Efficient Approach for Resource Sharing in Real-Time Multiprocessor Systems

div.p: Supporting resource sharing in multiprocessor architectures is one of the major problems that limit the potential performance benefits of using such architectures for real-time systems. Many approaches and algorithms have been proposed to support resource sharing, however, most of them impose either high blocking times on tasks or require a large memory allocation. In this paper we investigate the possibility of combining the lock-based approaches and wait-free approaches (using multiple buffers) in order to decrease both the blocking times that may affect the schedulability of tasks and the required memory. To achieve this, we propose a solution based on evaluating the maximum allowed blocking time on each task according to the schedulability analysis, and then find the minimum memory allocation for each resource that limits the blocking times on tasks to be less than the maximum allowed blocking times.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Due to the problems with power consumption and related thermal problems, processor architects are moving toward multiprocessor (multi-core) designs. A multi-core processor is a combination of two or more independent cores on a single chip, and multi-core is today the dominating technology for desktop computing. Real-time systems can benefit significantly from multi-core processors, as critical functionality can be assigned to dedicated cores, and independent tasks can execute concurrently to improve the performance and thereby enable new functionalities. Moreover, since the cores are located on the same chip and typically have shared memory, communication between cores is very fast. The performance improvements of using multi-core processors depend on the nature of the applications as well as the implementation of the software. To take advantage of the concurrency offered by a multi-core architecture, appropriate scheduling algorithms and synchronization protocols are required. However, in the real-time research community, scheduling has received much more attention than synchronization [1]. Thus there is a need for further research efforts to achieve efficient and adequate synchronization techniques.

In general, there are three approaches to manage resource sharing in multiprocessor architectures; the first and most popular approach is the lock-based approach (mutual exclusion). Using the lock-based approach, only one task is allowed to access the shared data (resource) at any time and no other task is allowed to access the shared resource until it is released by the locking task. This approach ensures the consistency of the shared data and also it is relatively simpler compared to other approaches. However, the main drawback of this approach is that it creates a priority inversion problem, i.e., a lower priority task that accesses a shared resource may block higher priority tasks in addition to the remote blocking from tasks located in different processors. These two types of blocking may not be bounded, causing tasks to miss their deadlines. Several synchronization protocols have been proposed to bound the blocking times imposed by the lock-based approach such as [2], [3], [4], [1]. However, in many cases the bounded blocking time might be too high causing tasks to miss their deadlines.

The second approach is the lock-free approach [5], [6]. Using the lock-free approach, multiple tasks are allowed to access shared data at the same time without blocking each others and tasks continue to execute until they require to write the results or take an action. To ensure the consistency of the shared data, a task checks whether the shared data was changed. If the data was changed then the task accesses the shared data again and repeats the same process until it succeeds to write the data. The main drawback of this approach in real-time systems is that it is not easy to bound the number of retries that a task needs in order to complete its execution over shared resources. Also the overhead of implementing this approach is higher than the other approaches.

The third approach is the wait-free approach [7] in which tasks do not interfere with each other when they access shared resources at the same time and they complete the operation on shared resources (read/write) in a bounded number of operations. The wait-free approach uses multiple buffers to avoid corruption of the data. The number of buffers required for each shared resource is proportional to the number of tasks that access the shared resource1 . As a result, the tasks that access shared resources may require more memory than the system can provide.

Note that, most embedded systems have limited resources. For certain systems, using the lock-based approach to synchronize accesses to shared resources may cause some tasks to miss their deadlines because of the high imposed blocking time while using the wait-free approach may not be feasible because of the limited memory size that the systems can provide.

In this paper, we propose an approach that is based on combining the lock-based and the wait-free approaches in order to decrease the blocking time on tasks and also to decrease the total required memory size. The basic idea is to provide fewer buffers for each shared resource compared to the case when the wait-free approach is used and as a result, tasks may still be blocked but the blocking time will be shorter than in the case where one buffer is used (lock-based).

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this paper, we assume that the multiprocessor (multi-core) platform is composed of identical, unit-capacity processors (cores) with shared memory.

The task set distributed on the multiprocessor consists of n periodic tasks, τ i (T i , C i , {Cs i,q,p }) where T i denotes the task period with worst-case execution time C i . The deadline of each job is equal to T i . The tasks allocated on processor P k share a set of resources, R. The set of shared resources (R) consists of two sets of different types of resources; local and global resources. A local resource is only shared by tasks on the same processor while a global resource is shared by tasks on more than one processor. The set of critical sections in which τ i accesses resources is denoted by {Cs i,q,p } where Cs i,q,p is the worst case execution time of p th critical section of task τ i in which the task locks resource R q ∈ R.

div.head: III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: Given a system with task set τ sharing R logical resources and partitioned in N processors and M em memory size available, find a synchronization protocol such that all tasks meet their deadlines (schedulable) and the maximum memory required for sharing resources M max will be M max ≤ M em. Figure 1 shows a simple example that explains the problem of sharing resources. If a lock-based approach is used then the blocking time on a task that accesses the shared resource will be B L and require M L memory. If the wait-free approach is used then the blocking time B W can be decreased (for some cases to zero) but the memory requirement M W will increase compared with the lock-based approach. However, for certain systems the maximum blocking time B max and memory size M max that guarantee the feasibility of the system can not be ensured using either lock-based or wait-free approaches, i.e., B max < B L and M max < M W .

By using a combination of lock-based and the wait-free (multiple buffers) approaches, the blocking time on tasks can be reduced and it becomes a function of the allocated memory B LW = f (M LW ), where B LW and M LW are the blocking time and memory allocation using the combined approach ( M max ≥ M LW ≥ M L ). The function f (M LW ) depends on the used lock-based and wait-free approaches since for each approach there are many algorithms proposed and unfortunately, there is no single optimal algorithm for all systems meaning that some algorithms are optimal for certain system setting and considerations [9].

Note that we may have a range of B LW and M LW that guarantees the schedulability of the tasks, and at the same time requiring less memory than M max . To find the optimal parameter setting for the approach, an optimization problem might be formulated and a cost function is required to be defined. It is clear that the more memory provided, the shorter the blocking time will be on tasks which in turn decreases the response time of the tasks. However, we keep this as future work and present here a simpler approach by finding the minimum memory size which guarantees the schedulability of all tasks.

div.head: IV. THE APPROACH
div.p: In this paper, we propose an approach similar to the one presented in [10] for a single processor system. Let us first assume that a task τ i is blocked by one shared resource R j . We then find the maximum safe blocking time B max i,j that the task can tolerate without missing its deadline (maximum slack), depending on the schedulability analysis of the hosting processor. Based on the value of B max i,j we find the minimum memory size M i,j that makes blocking time on τ i to be less than or equal to B max i,j . For each shared resource R j , the memory size required is M (R j ) = max ∀τi (M i,j ). Then

Note that in single processor systems, a task may only be blocked one time by a lower priority task when a proper synchronization protocols is used (such as Priority Ceiling Protocol PCP [11]). Unfortunately, for multiprocessor systems, and depending on the synchronization protocol in use, a task can be blocked several times during its execution by tasks that share different resources. The problem becomes more complex as the blocking time on a task will not be the maximum blocking time imposed by lower priority tasks but it will be the summation of all possible blocking times. In this case we may use an iterative approach to decrease the maximum blocking time on the task under consideration, i.e, providing more memory to the resource that causes the maximum blocking time on that task. This approach might not give the optimal results. However, its simplicity is attractive.

Another interesting observation concerning multiprocessor real time systems with lock-based synchronization is that the remote blocking from tasks that are located in different processors might be dominant. For many cases, it might be enough to decrease or eliminate its effect to make tasks schedulable. Taking this into account, it might be possible to use multiple buffers between processors and the lock-based approach within each processor. This means that we may be able to control which tasks may block each others to decrease the blocking time.

V. RELATED WORK Looking at the lock-based approach in the domain of single processors, two of the well known synchronization protocols are PCP (Priority Ceiling Protocol) [11] and SRP (Stack-based Resource allocation Protocol) [12]. For multiprocessor systems, Rajkumar presented MPCP [13], which extends PCP [11] to multiprocessors for synchronization of tasks sharing mutually exclusive resources using Partitioned Fixed Priority Scheduling (P-FPS). MSRP (Multiprocessor SRP) was proposed by Gai et al. [3], [4] which is a P-EDF (Partitioned EDF) based synchronization protocol for multiprocessors and it extends SRP to multiprocessors. Block et al. [1] proposed Flexible Multiprocessor Locking Protocol (FMLP) which can be applied to both partitioned and global scheduling algorithms, i.e., P-EDF and G-EDF. Easwaran and Andersson have proposed a synchronization protocol [14] under the global fixed priority scheduling protocol. In this paper, the authors have derived schedulability analysis of the Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) under global scheduling algorithms. Recently Nemati et al. [9] have proposed a locking protocol for resource sharing among independently-developed applications on multiprocessors. Each application, which is allocated on a dedicated processor, is represented by an interface that abstracts the resource requirements of the system.

In the context of the wait-free synchronization multiple buffers are used to avoid tasks from being blocked and having to wait for shared resources. Several approaches have been proposed to bound the number of required buffers. Simpson [15] considered the case of multi-readers and multiwriters access to shared resources and showed that the number of buffers required is 2 × n w × (n r + 1), where n w is the number of readers and n r is the number of writers. Chen and Burns [16] proposed an algorithm to decrease the number of buffers to n r + 2 for systems that have single writer and multiple readers. The proposed approach is based on the use of a consensus protocol between the writer and the readers to avoid any corruption of the data while a task is reading from a buffer. The approach also avoids the scenario when reading from a buffer that another task is currently writing to. Tsigas and Zhang [17] presented an algorithm that decreases the number of buffers to n w + n r + 1 for the case of multiple readers and multiple writers. However, the algorithm is limited to the case when the writer task has the highest priority in its processor and also it includes retry loops.

Other approaches to bound the number of buffers were proposed by Chen and Burns [8] and Choet al. [18] by using the timing properties of tasks and assuming the case of single writer and multiple readers. The approach presented in [8] was generalized including multiple writers in [19].

Combining different approaches for synchronization have been studied before. Kopetz and Reisinger [5] used buffers to bound the numbers of retry loops of a lock-free approach. Baruah proposed a combined approach of multiple buffers and a lock-based synchronization in [10] to limit the blocking time on tasks executed in a single processor. The same principle has been used recently by Di Natale et al. in [20] where an optimization problem is formulated to decrease the time delay and the memory requirement for tasks executed in a single processor. Finally an adaptive mechanism has been proposed by Usui et al. in [21] that combine both lock-based and lock-free approaches. During runtime, the mechanism decides which approach should be used (lock-free or lock-based) to increase the efficiency of the system, however, this work does not provide any real-time guarantees.
The main idea proposed in this paper is similar to the work of Baruah [10] and Di Natale [20], however, unlike these works we are targeting multi-processor real-time systems.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, we have proposed a new synchronization approach for real-time tasks executing in a multiprocessor platform. The proposed approach combines lock-based and wait-free synchronization and protection of shared resources. The goal with our approach is to reduce the blocking time imposed by a pure lock-based solution and at the same time reduce the memory requirements for a pure wait-free approach. The new approach will be applicable to real-time systems that have limited resources in terms of memory and timing where neither exclusive lock-based and wait-free synchronization is feasible. In addition, the proposed approach might be suitable for more general real-time systems, since the performance of the systems can be optimized, for example, decreasing the response time of tasks while using less memory.

Our ongoing work includes defining the blocking-time as a function of memory f (M LW ) for different lock based approaches such as M P CP, F M LP, M SRP, ... and different wait-free algorithms, and compare the results of each combination. In addition, we would like to investigate the best implementation for the proposed approach with minimum overhead. Furthermore, generalizing the multiprocessor schedulers by including global schedulers is another intersecting research direction. Finally, we are interested in formulating an optimization problem and defining a cost function based on timing requirements and memory limitation to find the optimal setting for the proposed approach.
